misconception.description: inverting the ratio and dividing operating profit by contribution, which reports the profit margin on contribution instead of how sensitive profit is to sales

worked_example.text: A workshop sells 5,000 units at EUR 40 with a variable cost of EUR 24, and has fixed costs of EUR 40,000.
worked_example.solution: Contribution = 5,000 x 16 = EUR 80,000. Operating profit = 80,000 - 40,000 = EUR 40,000. Degree of operating leverage = 80,000 / 40,000 = 2.00, so a 10% rise in sales lifts profit by 20%.

problem.text: A manufacturer sells 10,000 units a year at EUR 50 each, with a variable cost of EUR 30 per unit and fixed costs of EUR 120,000. What is its degree of operating leverage?

distractors.note: the documented misconception: the ratio inverted, which reports a margin rather than a sensitivity
using the fixed costs on top instead of the contribution

hints: Operating leverage compares two quantities the business already has: what all its sales contribute, and what is left of that after the fixed costs. Work out both before forming any ratio.
Total contribution is the units sold times the margin on each. Operating profit is that contribution minus the fixed costs, so it is always the smaller of the two.
The degree of operating leverage is contribution divided by operating profit, the larger over the smaller, so the answer is always greater than one when the firm is profitable.
worked_solution: Step 1: the margin on a unit is 50 - 30 = EUR 20, so total contribution is 10,000 x 20 = EUR 200,000. Step 2: operating profit is 200,000 - 120,000 = EUR 80,000. Step 3: the degree of operating leverage is 200,000 / 80,000 = 2.50. It reads as a multiplier: a 10% rise in sales would lift operating profit by 25%, and a 10% fall would cut it by the same. Dividing the other way round would give 0.40, which is the share of contribution that survives the fixed costs, a different and much less useful number.

near_transfer.text: A firm with a degree of operating leverage of 2.5 expects sales to grow by 10% next year. By what percentage should its operating profit grow?

distractors.note: assuming profit grows in step with sales, which is true only with no fixed costs
dividing by the leverage instead of multiplying by it

far_transfer.text: A company reports total contribution of EUR 600,000 and fixed costs of EUR 450,000. What is its degree of operating leverage?

distractors.note: fixed costs on top instead of contribution
